title: Pentecost
hook: the golden sequence: come, father of the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ascension, and the apostles staring at the sky. Your line was the work is ours now. What did you do that was yours to do? Day six hundred seventy.

The apostles are gathered in one place with Mary and some of the women, praying and waiting. Jerusalem outside is full of pilgrims for a harvest festival, the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover. Then, Acts says, a sound from heaven like a mighty wind fills the whole house, and something appears like tongues of fire, resting on each one of them. They spill out into the street speaking, and a crowd gathered from many nations hears them, each in their own language. Centuries later, someone wrote a song for this day that the Church still sings before the Gospel.
screen: `TOGETHER IN ONE PLACE.` → `WIND, AND TONGUES OF FIRE.` → `A SONG FOR THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Pentecost comes from the Greek for fiftieth: fifty days after Easter, the way the Jewish feast of weeks falls fifty days after Passover. Acts describes it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire." On this day the Mass has a sequence, an old poem sung after the second reading. The Missal's instructions require a sequence on just two days: Easter, and this one. It's called the golden sequence, and it's usually credited to Stephen Langton, an archbishop of Canterbury, though nobody can prove he wrote it. It opens in Latin: "Veni, Sancte Spiritus." Come, Holy Spirit. Then a run of lines, each one calling the Spirit by a new name. The first is "Veni, pater pauperum." Come, father of the poor. Then giver of gifts, light of hearts, best comforter, the soul's sweet guest. Later verses ask the Spirit to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is stiff, warm what is cold. Notice where it starts. Of all the names it could have used first, it chose the poor. Not the powerful, not the learned. In Acts, the Spirit fell on a roomful of ordinary people, fishermen among them, and a few verses later the new community is selling what it owns and dividing it, as anyone had need. The sequence remembers that, and puts the poor at the head of its list.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.` · `THE GOLDEN SEQUENCE.` · `IT STARTS WITH THE POOR.` · then, large: `VENI, PATER PAUPERUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come, Holy Spirit. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one place in you that's dry, or cold, or stiff: a resentment, a tiredness, a door you've closed. Don't fix it. Just bring it to mind. If you pray, you can say the old opening words on your breath, in Latin or English: Veni, Sancte Spiritus. Come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, simply breathe in as if you were opening a window in that room. The bell holds the time.
Pentecost. Greek for fiftieth: the day fifty days after Easter when tongues of fire rested on the apostles and the golden sequence calls the Spirit by many names. Today's word.
Your line: come, father of the poor. Today, notice one person who has nothing to bring, and bring them something: time, a meal, your attention. Day six hundred seventy.

howItsDone: On Pentecost Sunday Catholics wear red at Mass, hear the story of the Spirit's coming in Acts 2, and sing or recite the sequence Veni, Sancte Spiritus before the Gospel; the Easter season ends that day.

myth: the Church requires a sequence at every Sunday Mass
only two are required all year: at Easter and at Pentecost.
the sequence's first name for the Spirit is father of the poor
veni, pater pauperum comes right after the opening call.
we know for certain who wrote the golden sequence

fork.setup: you're writing a song to call on the Holy Spirit. you've opened with come, Holy Spirit. which name comes next in the real sequence?
fork.reveal: veni, pater pauperum: come, father of the poor. of all the names it could choose first, it chose the poor.

original.note: Latin: come, Holy Spirit — the opening of the Pentecost sequence.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pentecost is about speaking in tongues.
what it means: the Spirit comes on the fiftieth day, and the Church sings a sequence that calls him father of the poor.
what a scholar hears: one of only two required sequences, usually credited to Stephen Langton, though authorship is uncertain.

notes: Required sequences: Easter (Victimae paschali laudes) and Pentecost (Veni, Sancte Spiritus); Lauda Sion and Stabat Mater optional. Confirm.
Authorship: commonly attributed to Stephen Langton (d. 1228); other attributions exist (Innocent III). Stated as uncertain.

English renderings of the sequence's names (giver of gifts, light of hearts, best comforter, sweet guest; wash, water, heal, bend, warm) are the writer's own literal translation of the Latin, not a quoted translation; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer repeats day 669's nine days or calls the room locked (that's John 20); 'a dozen countries' and 'twelve hundred years' cut; 'first thing the community did was share' corrected to Acts 2:44–45; required-sequence fact now sourced to GIRM 64; Langton's death year cut; closing line attributed to the sequence, not stated as fact.
